transcript:
Meeting header: Date: 2027-06-25 | Start: 16:00 UTC | Duration: 42 minutes | Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Evelyn Cruz (Redwood Marketing), Samir Rao (Redwood SE), Laura Chen (VP Product, Solaris), Diego Martinez (CTO, Solaris), Priya Nair (Lead ML Engineer, Solaris), Marcus Lee (Head CS, Solaris)

[00:00] Maya Patel: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. This is Maya from Redwood, and Evelyn from our marketing team is here — Evelyn, do you want to do a quick intro and how we'll use this recording?

[00:18] Evelyn Cruz: Yeah, hi all, thanks so much. We're doing a short customer interview — it will be a mix of conversational Q&A and a couple of soundbites we're hoping to use in a blog post and short social clips. We'll share the draft before publishing. Feel free to tell us if anything is sensitive.

[00:35] Laura Chen: Sounds good. We just want to make sure the logo usage and some of the cost numbers are checked with finance. But we're excited to talk.

[00:43] Diego Martinez: Yep, hi, thanks. I'm Diego, CTO. Priya's on the tech details. Marcus here for CS perspective.

[00:49] Priya Nair: Hi everyone.

[00:52] Maya Patel: Great. We'll start with a quick timeline question: when did Solaris first evaluate Redwood and what was the first use case?

[01:05] Laura Chen: So we started looking late 2025, early 2026. The first use case was in-product personalization, like content ranking within our B2B dashboard. We needed sub-100ms responses for interactive filtering, and cost had to stay predictable.

[01:24] Samir Rao: Can you say more about the predictability constraint — was it budget-based or throughput-based?

[01:30] Laura Chen: Both. We have a big seasonal peak — Q4 — so we needed something that wouldn't explode spend when usage spiked. Also, some of our customers are quite latency-sensitive, so the balance mattered.

[01:42] Diego Martinez: To add, we had a previous attempt to host open models ourselves. The ops burden and weird latency spikes made it hard to rely on. We wanted something that felt production-ready with fallback options.

[01:55] Evelyn Cruz: When you first tried Redwood, was the Hosted API the fit or did you go straight to a dedicated deployment?

[02:04] Priya Nair: We piloted on Hosted API for a month to validate model selection and prompt design, then moved to Redwood Dedicated when we saw steady traffic and needed assured throughput and isolation.

[02:15] Maya Patel: Nice. Can you share any concrete metrics about latency, cost, or quality improvements after switching?

[02:24] Laura Chen: Sure. Our P50 latency went from around 320ms to about 85ms in the Dedicated pool with batching and prefix/kv cache optimizations. Cost per 1k tokens went down roughly 34% after enabling recommended quantization and batching profiles.

[02:41] Marcus Lee: From CS side, the error rates dropped, too. We used to see occasional 5xx bursts during scaling events; post-migration, those have become rare — maybe 0.1% during peak.

[02:55] Samir Rao: Did you use Redwood's automatic routing/fallback for cross-region failover at all?

[03:02] Diego Martinez: Yes, that's one of the surprising wins. We had a small outage in one region and the automated fallback to a nearby region kept the feature live, albeit with a minor latency bump. The customers didn't notice.

[03:18] Evelyn Cruz: That's a great quote, maybe we can use that in the blog.

[03:22] Laura Chen: Yeah, use it.

[03:25] [small chuckle, cross talk]

[03:30] Maya Patel: Let's talk about integration. How long did the engineering work take and were there surprises?

[03:36] Priya Nair: The integration was about three sprints for our team — two engineers part time. The SDKs were straightforward. Biggest surprise was tuning the cache heuristics for our prefix-heavy prompts — we initially mis-tuned and had some cache thrash. Samir actually helped us with custom TTLs and batching windows which fixed it.

[04:02] Samir Rao: Glad that helped. We sometimes see the transcription or telemetry label mis-read model names — people write 'Redwood Dedicatede' in notes, so we standardized naming in the repo.

[04:15] Diego Martinez: (laughs) Yeah we had that in our changelog — typos galore.

[04:20] Maya Patel: Were there any security or compliance requirements that influenced the deployment choice?

[04:27] Laura Chen: Yes — we needed SOC2 and audit logs at a minimum, and in a couple accounts we had to ensure data residency. The availability of Redwood Private for a subset of clients was key. For most production flows we use the Dedicated pool within our preferred cloud region and keep PII out of prompts.

[04:49] Marcus Lee: Also, the RBAC and token-level controls made rollout to customer success much smoother — we could limit what CS could do in prod.

[04:58] Evelyn Cruz: On the customer-facing side, do you have a favorite customer quote or anecdote since the migration?

[05:06] Laura Chen: One partner ran a live demo to 200 enterprise users and the interactive search didn't stutter once. That was an eye-opener for us.

[05:14] Diego Martinez: I can add a quick technical anecdote: we reduced cold-start latency by persisting warmed KV cache snapshots across instance restarts — some of that was facilitated by Redwood's cache export tooling, which saved us about 40ms on average.

[05:32] Priya Nair: Right, although early docs called it "KV cash" in one place and that confused our new hires — small typo but funny.

[05:42] Maya Patel: (laughs) We'll make sure our copy team doesn't print that.

[05:48] Evelyn Cruz: Switching gears — are there measurable business outcomes beyond latency/cost? Conversion uplift, retention signals?

[05:56] Laura Chen: We saw a 6% increase in feature engagement and a modest lift in trial-to-paid conversion for customers who experienced the personalized recommendations. It's attribution so caveats apply, but the A/B and holdout tests were significant at p<0.05.

[06:15] Marcus Lee: And support tickets related to 'slow search' dropped by about 28% in the first month after rollout.

[06:23] Maya Patel: That's strong. Were there any tradeoffs you had to accept? For example, model size vs latency, or quantization vs quality?

[06:33] Priya Nair: Yeah. We initially chose a mid-sized model with int8 quantization to hit latency targets. We saw a slight hit in long-tail hallucination rates for some complex prompts, so we introduced a reranking step using a smaller but more precise reranker. That brought quality back up without blowing the budgets.

[07:00] Diego Martinez: Also policy: some internal stakeholders wanted everything on-prem, but the lift wasn't worth it for the non-sensitive flows, so we split: private for regulated customers, hosted/dedicated for the rest.

[07:13] Evelyn Cruz: For the blog, what tone works best — technical deep dive or more product-story-driven?

[07:20] Laura Chen: A hybrid. Start with the product story for the broader audience, include a technical sidebar or callout with metrics and a quote from Priya or Diego for the engineering audience.

[07:33] Maya Patel: Great. Priya, would you be comfortable being quoted on the technical choices?

[07:38] Priya Nair: Yes, happy to. Just want to sign off on the exact phrasing.

[07:42] Evelyn Cruz: We'll send the pull quotes and time stamps after this call. Anything you absolutely don't want published?

[07:50] Laura Chen: Just internal financial specifics and anything tied to pending contracts. Otherwise, we're good.

[07:57] Diego Martinez: Also please anonymize customer names in the examples if we mention them — we run a couple of comps that are sensitive.

[08:06] Maya Patel: Noted. Quick off-script question from Marcus: if we wanted a short video clip for the homepage, do you have a succinct single line about the impact?

[08:15] Marcus Lee: Hmm. "Redwood made our personalization feel instant at scale." That's one.

[08:22] Evelyn Cruz: Love that. We'll record that as a soundbite.

[08:26] [pause, typing noises]

[08:35] Maya Patel: Last thing — any advice for other product teams evaluating inference platforms?

[08:40] Laura Chen: Don't optimize only for model accuracy in isolation. Think about operational ergonomics: rollbacks, cache, autoscaling, and how the provider helps you in incidents. Those were the things that ended up saving us time.

[08:56] Priya Nair: And instrument early — collect the right telemetry for token distribution and sequence lengths. Those numbers drove our batching/quantization choices.

[09:08] Diego Martinez: Also, test failover and fallback policies — not just the happy path.

[09:15] Evelyn Cruz: Perfect. Thank you all. We'll follow up with the draft and clips. Anything else before we close?

[09:23] Laura Chen: No, thanks, excited to see the post.

[09:27] Diego Martinez: Thanks everyone.

[09:29] Priya Nair: Bye.

[09:31] Maya Patel: Thanks, bye.

[09:33] [call ends]

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings in tech terms (e.g., "KV cash" vs "KV cache"), some speaker labels simplified; timestamps approximate.
